item.title: Reengineering the Concept of Emergency Care
item.category: Academic emergency medicine : official journal of the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine
item.description:
Emergency departments (EDs) absorb most acute unscheduled care (AUC) in the United States. Routing all of this care through one high-intensity system serves no one well: crowding delays care for time-critical patients; visits that turn on evaluation and coordination, and routine and chronic care defined by longitudinal needs, are delivered episodically and at high cost in a setting built for resuscitation and stabilization; and clinicians trained for emergencies spend much of their time on work the category does not fit. I argue that this is not only a capacity or workflow problem but a conceptual one. In practice, "emergency care" is defined by arrival: crossing the ED threshold, not clinical risk, triggers the legal duties, insurance protections, and workflows attached to the label. This was no one's mistake; routing everything through the one door always open was a rational adaptation to a fragmented system. But the adaptation no longer merely persists; it forecloses alternatives. Using conceptual engineering, I trace how history, regulation, payment, public scripts, and lexical entrenchment stabilize this system, and situate it against the social drivers that make ED-as-default ethically necessary and operationally costly. I then propose an ameliorated concept of emergency care: a risk- and time-sensitive, expert-mediated, priority-conferring subset of AUC, determined by structured triage wherever it occurs. Because a definition changes nothing by itself, I outline a phased implementation pathway, show how it applies across delivery settings, including rural and safety-net systems where the ED should remain the local acute care hub, and describe the workforce implications for emergency medicine. The choice posed to the specialty is whether to keep treating crowding, mismatched care, and clinician dissonance as operational problems to optimize within the ED, or to recognize them as properties of what we mean by emergency care and of the system that enacts it.

item.title: PROMOTED-EM: Shifting Focus From Cataloging Barriers to Identifying Hidden Determinants of Advancement for Women in Academic Emergency Medicine
item.category: Academic emergency medicine : official journal of the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine
item.description:
Gender disparities in academic promotion persist despite decades of research documenting their scope. Women remain underrepresented at senior academic ranks in Emergency Medicine, with only 19% of full professors identifying as women. Existing literature has largely cataloged the barriers driving this gap-disproportionate clinical workloads, non-promotable labor burden, sponsorship deficits, and caregiving responsibilities-but has devoted comparatively little attention to the strategies women use to successfully navigate these barriers. This commentary proposes a shift in research focus: From documenting the problem to systematically studying the hidden determinants of advancement among women who have achieved promotion. We introduce PROMOTED-EM, a qualitative research framework organized across 14 domains of academic career life, designed to elicit the tactical, behavioral, and relational strategies that enabled promotion. By centering the experiences of successfully promoted women in Emergency Medicine while explicitly attending to intersectionality and the limitations of survivor bias, this agenda aims to generate actionable, evidence-based guidance for women faculty, department leaders, and institutions committed to closing the promotion gap.

Landry A, Rohra A, Sun WW, Moreira M, Coates WC

item.title: Risk Stratification of Acute Pulmonary Embolism: Outcomes in Patients With Intermediate sPESI Scores and Negative Cardiac Biomarkers
item.category: Academic emergency medicine : official journal of the Society for Academic Emergency Medicine
item.description:
Background: Current pulmonary embolism (PE) guidelines support outpatient management for selected low-risk patients, typically identified using the simplified Pulmonary Embolism Severity Index (sPESI). The prognostic value of individual sPESI scores in the direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) era, particularly when combined with cardiac biomarker assessment, remains uncertain.

Research question: To evaluate 7-day and 30-day all-cause mortality among patients with acute PE, sPESI scores of 2 or 3, and negative cardiac biomarkers treated with a DOAC.

Study design and methods: Retrospective cohort study of US adults diagnosed with acute PE in a VA emergency department and prescribed a DOAC within 24 h of diagnosis at any U.S. Veterans Affairs (VA) Health System from 2015 to 2024.

Main outcome measures: Seven-day and 30-day all-cause mortality.

Results: Of 6427 eligible patients, 1365 had an sPESI score of 2 and 455 had an sPESI score of 3 with negative cardiac biomarkers. In the sPESI 2 cohort, 7-day and 30-day mortality were 0.44% and 1.39%, respectively. In the sPESI 3 cohort, rates were 0.22% and 2.20%. Approximately 71% of sPESI 2 patients and 75% of sPESI 3 patients were hospitalized. Hospitalization was not associated with lower 7-day or 30-day mortality in either cohort.

Interpretation: Patients with acute PE, sPESI scores of 2 or 3, and negative cardiac biomarkers had low short-term mortality in this large, contemporary DOAC-treated cohort. These findings support prospective studies evaluating outpatient management in carefully selected patients.

Dore M, Duffy R, Melikechi O
Journal Article
